headline: India's Rice Prices Surge Despite Record Stocks of 55 Million Tonnes
subheadline: Southern premium varieties such as Sona Masoori have nearly doubled in a year after a weak monsoon, while the government's record reserves hold mostly common rice that southern consumers do not buy.
body:
• Rice prices in India rose 12.5% nationally in October from a year earlier, and some southern premium varieties have nearly doubled in a year — even though government stocks are at record levels.
  • India entered the new rice season on October 1 with 55.47 million metric tons in reserve, more than four times the buffer requirement, but the stocks are mostly common varieties that do not substitute for the premium rice the south eats.
  • Production is set to fall for the first time in a decade after the weakest monsoon in more than a decade, while poultry feed and ethanol makers are competing for broken rice.
  • For diaspora shoppers: India supplies nearly 40% of global rice trade, so any export curbs New Delhi imposes to cool prices at home could tighten supplies of varieties such as Sona Masoori in overseas Indian stores.

Prices of some rice varieties popular in southern India have nearly doubled over the past year, pushing the national average up 12.5% in October from a year earlier even as government stocks sit at record levels, according to a Reuters explainer. The increase lifted food inflation to its highest level in nearly two years, complicating New Delhi's efforts to contain prices as milk, pulses, sugar and vegetables also become more expensive.

A weak monsoon, felt unevenly

A drop in overall rice production and rising demand for broken rice are driving prices higher. Production is set to fall for the first time in a decade, marking the steepest decline in nearly 20 years, as the lowest monsoon rain in more than a decade hit crops during the critical grain-maturity stage, cutting yields.

The impact, however, has been uneven. Southern states bore the brunt of the rainfall deficit, which significantly affected output of premium non-basmati varieties such as Seeraga Samba, Sona Masoori, HMT and BPT, widely consumed in the region. Prices of some of these grades have nearly doubled over the past year, while varieties popular in other parts of the country recorded more modest gains. It is that rally in southern India's preferred varieties that has pushed up the national average price of rice.

Broken rice has new buyers

Adding to the pressure, broken rice is seeing stronger demand from poultry and cattle feed manufacturers and ethanol producers, besides its traditional use in food processing. With corn prices hitting record highs amid a production shortfall and the government restricting sugar diversion for ethanol, these industries are turning to broken rice as an alternative, intensifying competition for supplies and driving up prices.

Why record stocks are not taming prices

India entered the new rice season on October 1 with record rice stocks of 55.47 million metric tons, more than four times the government-set buffer requirement. However, the massive reserves largely comprise common rice varieties that cannot easily substitute for the premium non-basmati varieties preferred by consumers in southern states, where prices have surged, says B.V. Krishna Rao, president of the Rice Exporters Association. That mismatch between the composition of government stocks and regional consumption preferences has limited the impact of abundant supplies on retail prices.

What New Delhi could do next

India could impose a 20% export duty on non-basmati rice shipments, reintroduce a floor price, or minimum export price, or even prohibit exports of 100% broken rice, as it did in 2022, to divert more supplies to the domestic market. India, the world's largest rice exporter, accounts for nearly 40% of global trade.

On the supply side, New Delhi could offer more rice from its inventories to private buyers, after doubling its target earlier this month to 5 million tons. Additional supplies of subsidised rice through state-run outlets could also improve retail availability and ease price pressures. The government could also tighten controls on private inventories, building on weekly stock disclosure requirements after allowing five southern states to impose stock limits; tighter restrictions and tougher enforcement could curb hoarding.

A targeted fix, not a blanket ban

Because the price surge has been concentrated in a handful of premium non-basmati varieties, government intervention could be narrowly targeted rather than applied across the board, limiting disruption to India's wider export trade. Higher export taxes could also erode India's price competitiveness overseas, giving an advantage to rival suppliers such as Thailand, Vietnam and Pakistan, which have struggled to compete with cheaper Indian rice.

key_takeaways: India's rice prices surged 12.5% nationally in October, with some premium southern varieties nearly doubling.
Record government rice stocks of 55.47 million tonnes are mostly common varieties, not matching premium demand.
A weak monsoon, the lowest in over a decade, caused the first production fall in a decade.
Increased demand for broken rice from poultry feed and ethanol makers is driving up prices.
India, supplying 40% of global rice, may impose export curbs, impacting overseas Indian stores.
